problem: Frontier-candidate zero-shot ObjectNav methods make redundant point-level decisions (several frontiers lead to the same navigable direction) with only indirect evidence about unexplored branches. Topology-aware methods such as VoroNav still pay a fixed 360° panoramic scan at every junction and reconsider already traversed rear directions.
motivation: Human wayfinding research shows intersections are decision points where people gather information before committing to a route. Point-level frontier choices and full panoramic scans waste steps on rotation and revisits, which hurts path efficiency (SPL). Open-vocabulary grounding also suffers from false positives and missed targets.
key_idea: Organize exploration around persistent, FMM-path-induced directions, inspect only newly revealed forward directions within a 240° range to obtain representative views, and reuse those views for VLM direction selection, prompt enrichment for SAM3, and cross-frame verification.
insight: Directional structure is the main source of efficiency: on common successful episodes with start-to-goal distance over 10 m, DRIVE-Nav needs 133.4 steps and 0.132 revisits, versus 222.1 steps for direction inspection with a 360° scan and 163.5 steps / 0.364 revisits for VLFM. Swapping the grounding backbone from OWLv2+MobileSAM to SAM3 gives only +0.7 SR / +1.2 SPL, so most of the remaining gain comes from prompt enrichment and verification (46.3/27.5 to 50.2/32.6). Weighted FMM and the 240° inspection each contribute (removing either lowers SR/SPL).
method: Path-induced direction candidates: weighted FMM (obstacle-avoidance speed times Voronoi-skeleton-preference speed, λ=0.65, β=3.0) recovers a path to each frontier. The bearing is taken where the path first crosses a robot-centered circle of radius 0.8 m.

Direction clustering and temporal association: bearings are sorted circularly and greedily grouped while the span stays below 45°, starting after the largest gap. Persistent labels are kept via position-based merging and greedy angular matching by circular distance.

Tracked-direction view acquisition: the agent follows the farthest frontier in the selected direction until new forward exits appear. It then rotates only as far as needed to face directions within ±120° (the 240° forward set) that lack views, and records a representative view when the yaw error is under 15°.

Semantic direction selection: Qwen3-VL-8B looks at the representative views to choose the next direction and to judge whether the target is visible. If it is, the robot turns toward the target-bearing direction.

Direction-guided prompt enrichment: when the VLM sees the target but SAM3 returns no mask, the two alternate for up to 5 rounds. The VLM proposes detector-oriented noun phrases from the view, the stored direction description and previously failed prompts; SAM3 tests each, and the successful phrase is cached.

Cross-frame verification: over at most 3 approach frames, Qwen3-VL sees the RGB image, the mask overlay and earlier frames, and answers completely sure / uncertain / definitely not. Accepted masks go into the object map, and rejected ones are stored as failed-position memory.

setting.backbone: Qwen3-VL-8B (frozen, reasoning) + SAM3 (frozen, detection/segmentation); Qwen3-VL-4B on the real robot
setting.action_space: low-level Habitat actions following FMM planned paths to frontiers; max 500 steps

numbers.extra: Split assumed to be val-unseen; the paper says only 'full HM3D-OVON validation set (3000 episodes)'
numbers.evidence: Table 1 comparison: HM3D-OVON SR 50.2 / SPL 32.6; Table 4 full system 50.2/32.6

numbers.method: Directional reasoning only (no prompt enrichment, no verification)

numbers_note: The paper does not name the exact splits for any benchmark (HM3D-OVON is just 'full validation set, 3000 episodes'), so the split labels are assumptions. HM3Dv2 has no canonical benchmark name and is labeled 'other'. No NE or other metrics are reported.
results: DRIVE-Nav reaches 50.2% SR / 32.6% SPL on HM3D-OVON, beating MSGNav (48.3/27.0) by 1.9 SR and 5.6 SPL. It has the best SPL on HM3Dv1 (35.9), HM3Dv2 (41.3) and MP3D (22.6), beating ApexNav by 2.9, 3.3 and 4.8 SPL respectively. Its SR is below ApexNav on HM3Dv1 (55.5 vs 59.6) and HM3Dv2 (72.4 vs 76.2).
limitations: Real-world evaluation is only qualitative demos on 5 categories with a Unitree G1 humanoid, with no baselines or large-scale benchmarking; LiDAR frontier instability causes transient direction reconsideration.
Relies on heavy foundation models (SAM3 ~270 ms per step, Qwen3-VL direction selection ~8 s), with offboard computation.
The system is not evaluated in dynamic scenes and has no episodic memory for revisitation-aware planning.
